summary: A tale of a predator's hunger and a child's misplaced trust, in which curiosity and fear mount question by question until the teeth.

need-to-breathe.why: In the Grimm version the girl and her grandmother are swallowed whole and come out of the wolf's belly alive, saying how dark it was inside, but suffocation is not dwelt on.

hungry.why: The wolf, who has not eaten for three days in Perrault, hungers for the girl and the grandmother and devours both; the basket of cake and butter is for the ailing grandmother.

full.why: In Grimm the wolf, stuffed with grandmother and girl, falls asleep snoring loudly, which is how the huntsman finds him.

thirsty.why: The second Grimm wolf is tempted by the smell of sausage water in the trough and drowns reaching for it; otherwise no one thirsts.

sleepy.why: The sick grandmother lies in bed, and the glutted wolf sleeps so soundly that the huntsman can cut him open without waking him.

fatigued.why: The wolf races ahead and the girl dawdles; no one tires.

pain.why: The wolf's belly is cut open and sewn full of stones, and he collapses dead when he tries to flee, while in Perrault both victims are simply eaten.

disgusted.why: The wolf in the grandmother's nightcap, with his hairy arms and great teeth, repels the girl, and the Grimm victims emerge from his belly, but revulsion is faint.

afraid.why: The girl grows afraid as she notes the wolf's great arms, ears, eyes, and teeth, and in Grimm feels a strange dread at the open door; the wolf is the predator every child fears.

anxious.why: The mother in Grimm warns the girl not to leave the path, and the girl feels uneasy when she finds the cottage door open and her grandmother looking strange.

panic.why: The wolf springs from the bed and swallows the girl in one gulp; there is no time for flight or panic.

sensory-pleasures.why: In Grimm the wolf points out the sunbeams, birdsong, and pretty flowers, and the girl wanders deeper into the wood gathering them.

aesthetic-pleasures.why: The girl is drawn by the beauty of the wildflowers, and that is the only aesthetic note.

fun-excitement.why: Perrault's girl amuses herself gathering nuts, chasing butterflies, and picking flowers while the wolf takes the shorter road, and Grimm's dawdles among the blossoms.

love-romantic.why: Perrault's verse moral turns the wolf into a gentle seducer who follows young ladies into their chambers, but the tale itself has no romance.

love-family.why: The whole errand is family care: the mother sends food to the sick grandmother, who had made the girl her red hood, and the girl goes willingly.

grief.why: No one is shown mourning; in Perrault the tale ends with the eating, in Grimm both victims are restored.

missing-someone.why: No separation is felt long enough to be missed.

aroused-sexually.why: Perrault's wolf bids the girl undress and climb into bed with him, a line his moral reads as seduction; the Grimm version drops it.

liking-as-a-friend.why: The girl chats with the wolf as with a friendly stranger, which is the trap; no real friendship exists.

empathy.why: The girl goes because her grandmother is ill and weak, and the huntsman, hearing the old woman's snoring, thinks to check on her.

compassion.why: Food for a sick grandmother, and in Grimm a huntsman who cuts the wolf open rather than shooting it so as to save the old woman, make caregiving the tale's frame.

grateful.why: After the rescue the grandmother eats the cake and drinks the wine and revives, and the three are content, but thanks are not spoken.

pleasure-from-helping.why: The huntsman is glad to have saved them and takes the wolf's skin home, pleased with his work.

trustful-distrustful.why: The girl trusts the wolf with her errand and her grandmother's address, the grandmother lets the false voice in, and the girl trusts the thing in the bed until the teeth.

depressed.why: No character lacks support in a way the tale dwells on.

angry.why: The huntsman calls the wolf an old sinner, but no character acts in anger.

jealous-friendship.why: There is no friendship to defend.

hatred.why: The huntsman has long sought this wolf, calling it an old sinner, and the second Grimm wolf is drowned without pity.

resentment.why: No norm violation is resented by a character.

proud.why: No one seeks or signals status.

amused.why: The ritual exchange about big ears, eyes, and teeth has a comic rhythm, and in Grimm's coda the girl and grandmother gleefully trick a second wolf into the trough.

lonely.why: The grandmother lives alone in the wood, which is why the wolf can reach her undefended.

judgy-moral-sense.why: Perrault appends a moral against trusting wolves, the Grimm huntsman names the wolf a sinner and kills him with stones, and the girl resolves never again to leave the path.

shame.why: In Grimm the girl, saved, blames herself for straying and vows to obey her mother, a flicker of shame.

guilt.why: The Grimm girl says to herself that she will never again run off the path when her mother has forbidden it.

sad.why: The grandmother is sick and weak, but no one is shown in sorrow.

happy.why: The Grimm tale ends with all three pleased, the grandmother revived by cake and wine and the girl safe, and begins with a cheerful errand.

joyful-euphoric.why: Little Red Riding Hood springs out of the wolf crying how frightened she was, and the three rejoice at their deliverance.

effort.why: Nothing in the tale is effortful.

focused-in-flow.why: No one is absorbed in a task.

distracted.why: The wolf lures the girl off the path with flowers, and she forgets her errand picking one blossom after another while he runs ahead.

impatient.why: The wolf runs ahead to the cottage by the shortest road, impatient to have both the grandmother and the girl.

curious.why: The wolf questions the girl about her errand and her grandmother's house, and the girl questions the creature in bed about its ears, eyes, hands, and teeth.

surprised.why: The girl is astonished at each of the wolf's features in turn, and the huntsman, cutting the belly open, is amazed to see a red hood appear.

skeptical-doubtful.why: The girl half-doubts the figure in the bed, question by question, and the huntsman thinks the old woman's snoring strange enough to look in.

feeling-of-knowing.why: No one strains to remember anything.

confused.why: The girl cannot work out why her grandmother looks and sounds so strange, and in Perrault she does not even know that wolves are dangerous.

frustrated.why: In Perrault the wolf dares not eat the girl in the wood because woodcutters are near, and must take the longer route of deceit.

uncertain-certain.why: The girl hesitates at the bedside, unsure what she is seeing, and the huntsman decides against shooting in case the grandmother is inside the wolf.

understanding.why: The exchange ends in the girl's dawning understanding at the word teeth, and the Grimm girl takes the lesson that the path is to be kept.

inspired.why: The wolf hits on the plan of going ahead and taking the grandmother's place, and in Grimm the grandmother thinks of the sausage water that drowns the second wolf.

satisfied.why: In Grimm the wolf falls dead of the stones, the huntsman takes the pelt, and all three are satisfied; in Perrault nothing is resolved.

foreboding.why: The mother's warning not to stray and the girl's unease at the open door and odd-looking grandmother foreshadow the trap.

anticipation-suspense.why: The wolf lies in bed waiting for the girl, and the dialogue delays the pounce question by question.

hope.why: No character hopes for anything beyond the errand.

schadenfreude.why: The girl and grandmother enjoy watching the second Grimm wolf slide off the roof into the trough and drown.

elevation.why: The huntsman's rescue is a good deed, but it is not felt as uplift by anyone.
